title: Does a Deterministic Runtime Verifier Improve LLM‑Driven NetOps Safety? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation and Diagnostic of an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1. The preregistered design used gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes), and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions). Confirmatory outcomes (from archived analysis artifacts) are exact and deterministic: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Diagnostics using execution and reconciliation artifacts show that shared_initial_generation together with reuse of the same deterministic validator created a deterministic ceiling that made the primary estimand uninformative in this run. We present the preregistered methodology, exact artifact‑grounded results, an operational diagnosis of the ceiling mechanism supported by provider_call_audit and validator traces, and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
LLM‑driven automation promises to translate operator intent into actionable network configuration workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback) with minimal human oversight. Prior studies demonstrate that LLMs can produce syntactically plausible configuration templates in controlled datasets and that verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops reduce deployment errors in infrastructure‑as‑code settings. These prior outcomes motivate an end‑to‑end operational question: when an LLM generator is paired with a runtime verifier in an agentic NetOps pipeline, does the verifier measurably increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline under a compact, action‑aware staged‑rollout benchmark?

We address this question with a fully preregistered paired binary experiment (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1) that isolates the verifier’s intervention on identical LLM outputs by design. The primary estimand is the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) measured on N=400 preregistered paired tasks. All execution, validator, and analysis artifacts were archived and form the sole basis for reported numbers and interpretation. The run produced a deterministic ceiling: every shared candidate passed deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions recorded 100% safe‑deploy (paired difference = 0.0). We report the preregistered design, the exact artifact‑grounded results, an evidence‑backed diagnosis of the ceiling mechanism, and concrete, actionable hardening recommendations that use items already present in the archived artifacts (task manifest difficulty labels, validator traces, and provider audit logs).
sections.related_work: Three literatures frame our study. First, intent→configuration generation: recent prototype systems and datasets show feasibility of translating natural‑language intent into network configuration artifacts but highlight dataset and generalization gaps; representative work includes intent‑to‑configuration demonstrations and pretrained/fine‑tuning efforts for configuration generation. Second, verifier‑guided workflows and deterministic verification: work on verifier‑guided IaC systems and deterministic network verifiers reports substantial reductions in syntactic/semantic errors offline, but explicit closed‑loop runtime integration and generator×verifier dynamics remain underexplored. Third, agentic/tool‑augmented architectures (ReAct/RAG/multi‑agent orchestration) expand capability but introduce failure modes (hallucination, misapplied tools, overconfidence) that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployments. Surveys and evaluation‑gap reviews repeatedly call for action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollout, repair, rollback, and provenance; our benchmark operationalizes these demands and, importantly, demonstrates a concrete statistical pitfall for paired evaluations when generation variance and deterministic scoring are conflated. The present paper contributes by executing a preregistered paired test under explicit shared‑generation semantics and then using the archived traces to explain why the design collapsed statistical signal despite clean execution.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The study preregistration (cnsmauto‑3d2k‑prereg‑v1) specified a paired binary confirmatory design with exactly N=400 paired tasks. The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; the prespecified primary test was a permutation‑based paired difference test. An exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap percentile CIs were prespecified as corroborating procedures. Secondary outcomes included bootstrap CIs for median time‑to‑rollback and counts of repair attempts.

Execution contract and critical design choices. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. The preregistration deliberately set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): for each task a single LLM candidate was generated and the identical candidate was routed to both baseline and guarded episodes. This reduced model‑call budget (model_calls_used = 400 for 800 episodes) and intentionally isolated the verifier’s acceptance decision on identical generator outputs. The adapter permitted up to one repair call in guarded episodes; repair_applied was recorded and remained false across the run.

Task generation, replay, and scoring. Tasks were produced by a seed‑controlled deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 that attaches structured difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). Deterministic replay checks were applied and passed for all pairs (no exclusions). Scoring and runtime blocking used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with full intent‑constraint validation; validator traces record validation_before/after, final_configuration, repair_applied, and validity decisions. All design choices, seeds, and analysis code were recorded in archived artifacts and used without manual adjudication.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run began 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z and completed 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed = 800; failed = 0. Model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation). Deterministic replay checks passed for every agent+simulator pair; no task was excluded.

Confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑grounded). Analysis artifacts report complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0); guarded_success_count = 400 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n_11 = 400 with n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0, yielding observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. The preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0; the exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Cohen’s h = 0.0. These values are reproduced exactly from the archived analysis outputs.

Repair, rollback, difficulty and provider diagnostics. Across all 800 episodes repair_applied = false and no rollbacks were invoked; validator traces show validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state for accepted configurations. Task manifest aggregation (artifact‑extracted) yields difficulty counts: medium: 80 tasks (20.0%); hard: 160 tasks (40.0%); very_hard: 160 tasks (40.0%). Deterministic_reconciliation/provider_call_audit records: hosted_model_call_event_count = 400, cache_miss_count = 400, stage_counts: {shared_initial_generation: 400}, condition_counts: {shared: 400}; all deterministic consistency checks passed. These records document the shared generation semantics and absence of cross‑condition model‑call variation.
sections.discussion:
Why the design produced a deterministic ceiling. Two preregistered choices together forced a deterministic ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation removed generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to both baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Under these conditions, whenever the deterministic validator accepted the shared candidate at runtime, the post‑hoc scoring necessarily recorded acceptance in both conditions; concordant acceptance across conditions is therefore forced by design and not informative about closed‑loop verifier utility.

Statistical and inferential interpretation. The primary‑test outputs (permutation p = 1.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, bootstrap CI point mass at zero) are correct and reflect the observed data, but they do not adjudicate whether a verifier would improve safety under a regime where generator and scorer variability are independent. The preregistered power rationale assumed a nontrivial baseline failure rate; that assumption was falsified by the frozen generator+validator pairing and thus the registered power calculations are not applicable to inference about generator×guard interactions in this run.

Operational implications and artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations. To preserve opportunities for runtime guards to accept, block, or request repair, evaluation designs must avoid conflating generator variance and scorer invariance. Using the archived artifacts (task manifest difficulty labels, validator traces, and provider_call_audit) we present concrete, implementable hardening steps:
(1) Independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true) so each condition receives an independent LLM candidate; this restores generator variance and avoids deterministic concordance forced by shared candidates.
(2) Distinct post‑hoc scorer or held‑out adjudicator (different implementation or a validator with controlled stochastic perturbation) so measurement does not trivially match runtime blocking rules.
(3) Controlled adversarial seeding: include seeded tasks designed to raise baseline failure rates (artifacts contain per‑task difficulty labels and patterns enabling targeted adversarial selection).
(4) Difficulty‑stratified sampling: enforce minimum sample sizes in very_hard strata (archives provide per‑task difficulty labels to deterministically resample tasks).
(5) Instrumented mitigation metrics (repair_attempts, repairs_applied, time‑to‑rollback) recorded and reported as numeric outcomes (validator traces already contain timestamps and repair_applied flags).
Each recommendation is actionable using items already present in the archived bundle and addresses the precise construct validity failure observed here.

Limitations and threats to validity. Internal validity in this run is reduced by shared generation and reuse of the same deterministic validator for runtime and scoring. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 models production checks deterministically and does not capture telemetry noise, asynchronous states, or stochastic adjudication policies. External validity is limited by the single generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and single deterministic validator; findings do not generalize to other model/verifier pairings. Adversarial robustness was not exercised and remains an open empirical question. The deterministic ceiling observed is a design artifact specific to the preregistered execution contract rather than evidence that verifiers are generally unhelpful.
sections.conclusion:
We implemented a fully preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline under ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions recorded 100% safe‑deploy across 400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). Deterministic concordance was caused by identical per‑pair generation and reuse of a deterministic validator for runtime blocking and post‑hoc scoring; this produced a deterministic ceiling that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and all execution/analysis artifacts and provide artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations (independent per‑condition generation, distinct scorer, adversarial seeding, difficulty stratification, and mitigation metrics) that restore opportunities for the verifier to intervene and enable meaningful inference about verifier utility in future runs. The archived artifacts contain the precise task manifest, validator traces, provider call audit, and analysis outputs required to implement the recommended hardening changes reproducibly and deterministically on the same benchmark corpus.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in the task manifest and can be aggregated by auditors; Table 1 reports the artifact‑extracted aggregated counts and percentages.
